The post Review: Wines of Adonna, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Adonna Wines is a new brand helmed by Japanese-American biochemist-turned-winemaker Donna Kato, who crafts California wines with an Asian sensibility. The goal: A focus on the vineyard and crafting an elegant finished product. The wines, for now, are only available to mailing list members, so check Adonna’s website if our coverage of its three 2026 releases sound appealing.

2024 Adonna Chardonnay Russian River Valley – Boldly infused with vanilla and coconut notes, this would come across as a prototypical Sonoma chardonnay if it wasn’t bottled at a mere 13.5% alcohol, which definitely helps with the acidity. Vibrant notes of lemon and some pear give this a higher fruit quotient than you might expect, with lychee emerging on the lengthy, slightly sweetened finish. Despite the suggestion of sugar, the wine is easy-drinking and quite versatile, and it paired wonderfully with grilled Korean-style chicken. A- / $85

2024 Adonna White Pinot Noir, Canfield Vineyard Russian River Valley – A rather rare expression of pinot noir produced sans skins and seeds, this white pinot is quite acidic and a bit vegetal, almost approaching a fino sherry with its gentle oxidation and ephemeral, lingering notes of pastoral greenery. There’s a certain cleansing quality to this wine, akin to the way you feel when drinking cucumber water at the spa. I like it in the moment — but only in the moment. B / $65

2023 Adonna Pinot Noir Russian River Valley – I can’t remember the last pinot noir I tasted that had this level of aggressive spice on it, the wine coming across with an impressively heavy hand that reaches into the breadth of the baking cabinet and backs it up with black cherries and plums. A shaving of pencil lead adds a gentle earthiness, which coaxes the finish into a slightly pruny posture as the spice starts to fade. Pinot rarely needs a lot of air time to reveal its charms, but this one is an exception that truly benefits from some retrospection. B+ / $85

title: Review: Mad River Burnt Rock Bourbon, Revolution Rye, and Double Tapped Maple Bourbon
summary:
At the southern end of Vermont’s Mad River Valley, in the town of Warren, Mad River Distillers has been making spirits since 2011. The distillery was founded with brandy in mind, not whiskey, but whiskey eventually became an important part of the operation. Today, Head Distiller Al Hilton oversees a whiskey program built around 100%…

The post Review: Mad River Burnt Rock Bourbon, Revolution Rye, and Double Tapped Maple Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
At the southern end of Vermont’s Mad River Valley, in the town of Warren, Mad River Distillers has been making spirits since 2011. The distillery was founded with brandy in mind, not whiskey, but whiskey eventually became an important part of the operation. Today, Head Distiller Al Hilton oversees a whiskey program built around 100% non-GMO grains grown in New York, Vermont, and Massachusetts.

That makes Mad River worth a closer look. Vermont whiskey can be an easy subject to oversimplify. Put a distillery in Vermont, source some local ingredients, put a maple reference on the label, and it can be tempting to call the result a Vermont whiskey story. Mad River offers something more substantive to examine. The location matters, but so do the decisions being made inside the distillery.

Fermentation runs for six days at 78 degrees Fahrenheit. Every whiskey is distilled on a pot still, beginning with a 500-gallon still for the stripping run before the spirit goes through a 66-gallon Müller pot still from Germany for the finishing run. The whiskey comes off the Müller at 150 to 158 proof, then enters 53-gallon barrels at 118 to 122 proof. Those barrels come from Kelvin Cooperage and receive a #3 char.

The barrels spend their time in a Vermont warehouse, some stored rick-style and others palletized. For most of the year, the building is essentially subject to the conditions outside, with only minimal heating during the Vermont winter.

There is a lot there to consider before a bottle ever reaches the glass. How much does Vermont’s climate matter? What does the choice of grains bring to the whiskey? And what happens when a relatively small distillery takes a process that could be described in fairly straightforward terms and applies it to three very different whiskeys?

Mad River sent samples of Burnt Rock Bourbon, Revolution Rye, and Double Tapped Maple Bourbon to Drinkhacker for review. Let’s find out what this small Vermont distillery has to offer.

Mad River Burnt Rock Bourbon Review

Burnt Rock Bourbon is a blend of two to three barrels, named after a popular hiking trail in Vermont’s Mad River Valley. It is distilled from a mashbill of 70% corn, 15% rye, and 15% smoked malted barley, with the barley smoked over maple wood. The youngest barrel in the blend is at least two years old, while the oldest barrels typically reach three to four years, putting the average age of the blend at 30 months.

The nose gets underway with maple-smoked bacon, bringing smoke and grease before moving toward holiday fruit cake, with dried orange peel taking the lead. From there, the aroma makes a clear turn toward black jelly beans and beet juice. It is an unusual combination, but an enjoyable one.

The palate opens with butterscotch pudding skin, offering sweetness alongside a slightly earthy quality. That sweetness fades quickly as grapefruit pith and leather take over the mid-palate. The finish brings bacon bits and heavily burnt orange peel, followed by a strong final push of over-baked corn tortillas. The slightly burnt youthful corn is potent.

At the moment, this comes across as something of a “vacation bottle,” one of those craft bourbon purchases made by a tourist during a trip that somehow never finds its way into the regular rotation once the bottle makes it home. The bourbon is still relatively young, and additional barrel time may help address some of the rough, grain-forward qualities that stand out at present. 92 proof. C+ / $58

Mad River Revolution Rye Review

Revolution is a blend of four to five barrels distilled from 100% organic rye. That 100% rye mashbill includes malted rye, malted and roasted rye, and unmalted rye. The youngest barrel in the blend is 18 months old, while the oldest is 24 months, giving the blend an average age of 22 months.

The nose starts with earthy roasted hazelnut before moving toward bright sliced green apples and pickled ginger. Given some time in the glass, aromas of caramelized onions and freshly pooled rainwater begin to appear. It is a pleasant nose, though the whiskey clearly presents as a young rye that could benefit from additional barrel time. There is plenty of promise here.

The palate opens with a hefty dose of chocolate-covered almonds, although it is difficult to pin down whether the note is closer to dark chocolate-covered almonds or almonds dusted with cocoa powder. The mid-palate brings potent minerality in the form of limestone gravel dust, with cream soda eventually joining the profile.

The mouthfeel is noticeably thick, creating an interesting sensation alongside the hefty limestone note. On the finish, that limestone gravel dust takes a more earthy turn, bringing to mind a freshly opened bag of potting soil. Freshly cut wet grass follows, along with mild chai spice and a strong final push of grapefruit pith.

Overall, there is plenty to like in this young, bright rye whiskey, but additional time in the barrel should allow the whiskey to develop further. I would like to revisit this distillate after it has spent four to five years in the barrel. 96 proof. B / $50

Mad River Double Tapped Maple Bourbon

Double Tapped Maple Bourbon is a cordial made from a blend of four to five barrels. The bourbon is distilled from a mashbill consisting of wheat, oats, corn, and malted barley. The youngest barrel in the blend is two years old, while the oldest is three to four years old. The bourbon is then blended with an undisclosed amount of “dark robust” maple syrup from central Vermont.

Historically, Vermont’s “Dark/Robust” category roughly corresponds to what consumers would have encountered as Grade A Dark Amber, a style typically harvested later in the season.

The nose opens with warm French toast and maple syrup, although the maple does not completely dominate. The spiced egg wash is equally apparent. After the initial rush of sweetness, sage and pine needles begin to show, accompanied by smoky brisket burnt ends. The maple syrup is certainly present, but it does not overwhelm the bourbon.

The maple becomes much more prominent on the palate. Candied yams arrive immediately, accompanied by plenty of maple syrup. The mouthfeel is noticeably thick and dense from the outset, leaving little doubt that some amount of maple syrup has been blended with the bourbon. The sweetness continues with pecan pralines and vanilla taffy, while tangerine zest provides some contrast through the mid-palate.

The finish adds oak to the sweet profile through pecan pie notes. Caramelized bananas bring another layer of sweetness before giving way to smoky bacon, with the smoky quality becoming stronger the longer the whiskey remains on the palate.

As a neat sipper, the thick mouthfeel and generally sweet profile are a bit too cloying for my preference. As a cocktail ingredient, however, there is more to work with. I would strongly consider it for a split-base Old Fashioned, with a high-proof rye whiskey serving as the larger spirit component. It could also work well in a lemon-forward whiskey sour. 76 proof.  B- / $48

summary:

With a heavy focus on Cabernet and Cab-heavy blends, these are big, opulent wines designed for special occasions, collecting, and potentially long-term cellaring. Let’s dig in to two 2023 releases from…

The post Review: 2023 Oleandri La Scala and Cabernet Sauvignon Rutherford appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Oleandri is a boutique Napa-based wine label that was new to me, but which I hope will become a regularly featured winery on Drinkhacker. With a heavy focus on Cabernet and Cab-heavy blends, these are big, opulent wines designed for special occasions, collecting, and potentially long-term cellaring.

Let’s dig in to two 2023 releases from the operation.

2023 Oleandri La Scala Red Wine Napa Valley – A Cabernet Sauvignon-heavy blend (67%) complemented by 20% Merlot, 8% Cabernet Franc, 4.5% Petite Sirah, and 0.5% Petit Verdot. Those additions take an already aggressive wine and make things even darker and denser, offering ink-black opacity and depth, immediately evoking currants tempered with chocolate, fresh vanilla bean, and some gravelly tannins. Earthy but not funky in the slightest, it’s a soulful wine that, with air time, leans into brighter cherry notes, complete with a touch of tempering acidity, and a soothing vanilla finish. Delightful. A / $80

2023 Oleandri Cabernet Sauvignon Rutherford – A dense (but not too dense) and chocolatey delight, this is an iconic example of Napa Cabernet made with some measure of restraint. In lieu of overt currant and blackberry notes, the wine showcases a more restrained plum-forward character alongside notes of fresh violets, with milk chocolate lingering on the finish and fading into notes of cafe au lait. This is a young cabernet that is ready to drink today, its tannins already well-mellowed and silky, adding a bit of body to the basket of fruit and flowers on display. A- / $200

title: Texas Wine Country Visits 2026, Part 2 – K Estate, Untamed, Adega Vinho, Grape Creek
summary:
I wasn’t planning to return to the wine rooms of Texas’s Hill Country, but a visit from my daughter prompted another day trip to the region, during which we visited four properties in this increasingly bustling area. As always, thoughts follow, along with some top picks to look out for. K Estate Part of the…

The post Texas Wine Country Visits 2026, Part 2 – K Estate, Untamed, Adega Vinho, Grape Creek appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
I wasn’t planning to return to the wine rooms of Texas’s Hill Country, but a visit from my daughter prompted another day trip to the region, during which we visited four properties in this increasingly bustling area. As always, thoughts follow, along with some top picks to look out for.

K Estate

Part of the sprawling Heath Family Wine operation (spanning five brands), K Estate operates a newly renovated but relatively small tasting room, with a focus on a broad swath of wines and styles. Most of these wines are not sold at retail. Wine club membership, as a result, is heavily promoted, but tasting here (a stand-at-the-bar affair) is perfectly pleasant, thanks to knowledgeable servers. Tastings include a small bowl of Heath’s herbed almonds, which are excellent palate cleansers.

Top Picks

2024 K Estate White – A blend of Marsanne, Roussanne, and Albarino sourced from estate grapes. A lovely balance between floral and lemon-driven notes greets the drinker, with soothing coconut lingering on the back end. $40

2023 K Estate Petit Verdot – Quite a surprise, as single-varietal Petit Verdot is rare in any region, and particularly Texas. This is a superstar offering, bursting with cherry and chocolate notes, barely hinting at florals. I also quite enjoyed the Malbec from K. $58

18421 E US-290, Stonewall, TX 78671

Untamed Wine Estates

This was an impromptu visit spurred by a desire to grab lunch, and give.

Given that Untamed’s restaurant has won numerous awards for its artisanal pizzas, this made for a natural place to stop. The owner’s history is South African, and its top-selling pie is inspired by the South African style, which includes bananas as a topping. I couldn’t convince the rest of my group to go for it, alas. Our more traditional pie, however, was a standout (and enough to feed three of us). The wines are mostly imported from California and South Africa, with just a tiny amount of Texas wine being served. Our server, Michael, was a real trip, sharing his love of wine and even bringing out blind samples to see whether we could guess the region and the grape (which, for once, I was successful at).

202 Ranch to Market Rd 1320, Johnson City, TX 78636

Adega Vinho

A Portuguese-inspired operation (“adega vinho” means “wine cellar” in the language), the tasting room here is a very different experience, with a boho thrift shop vibe that sees customers seated on couches dotting the quirky tasting room. Servers bring the operation’s universally light-bodied wines to the table and are likely to sit and chat for a spell before disappearing for the next bottle. During our visit, five wines were poured, many drawn from Hill Country grapes instead of the more common Texas High Plains fruit.

Top Pick

2023 Adega Vinho Chardonnay – Chardonnay is not typically thought of as a grape that thrives in Texas, but Adega Vinho does some wonders with it, turning out a shockingly on-point wine that could easily compete with anything from California. This is the only wine we actually purchased a bottle of during the trip (and drank it the next day). $45

1000 RM 1623, Stonewall, TX 78671

Grape Creek Vineyards

The pinnacle of the Heath Family operation is this unfortunately named but insanely popular operation that was packed to the gills when we arrived. The tasting rooms are somehow both luxurious and industrial and feature a series of stand-up bars that seems to never end — and again the wine club push is unrelenting. Service is efficient but, in my experience, a bit impersonal.

Top Pick

2023 Grape Creek Vineyards Bellissimo – A super Tuscan style wine blended from Cabernet Sauvignon and Sangiovese, the two grapes temper one another well in this hearty but exuberant offering. $60

10587 US-290, Fredericksburg, TX 78624

title: Review: Hard Truth Master Distiller’s Reserve Dark Roast Rye
summary:
Hard Truth Distilling is in Nashville, Indiana, although most visitors know the area simply as Brown County. That distinction matters here, because the name of Hard Truth’s latest rye seems almost tailor-made for its home. Brown County gives you the color, and Dark Roast gives you the whiskey. Released in September 2026, Hard Truth 2026…

The post Review: Hard Truth Master Distiller’s Reserve Dark Roast Rye appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Hard Truth Distilling is in Nashville, Indiana, although most visitors know the area simply as Brown County. That distinction matters here, because the name of Hard Truth’s latest rye seems almost tailor-made for its home. Brown County gives you the color, and Dark Roast gives you the whiskey.

Released in September 2026, Hard Truth 2026 Master Distiller’s Reserve Dark Roast Bottled in Bond Rye Whiskey is the third release in the distillery’s 2026 Master Distiller’s Reserve Series. Master Distiller Bryan Smith and his team selected 25 barrels, each aged for at least four years, and fermented the mash using Hard Truth’s sweet mash process. The final blend is divided evenly between two mashbills: RW-3 and RW-4.

Both mashbills begin with 51% rye and 38% corn. The remaining 11% is where things get interesting. RW-3 uses chocolate malt barley, while RW-4 uses caramel malt barley. Put the two together and you have a Brown County rye with not one, but two dark malted barleys behind its name.

So how did this Brown County blend turn out? Is Dark Roast worthy of its place as an annual limited release, and perhaps worthy of a trip to the distillery itself?

Hard Truth Master Distiller’s Reserve Dark Roast Bottled in Bond Rye (2026) Review

The nose opens with cold brew coffee, not overly strong but clearly present, alongside sweetened cocoa powder. As the rye opens further, cinnamon graham crackers make a noteworthy showing, followed by the combined impression of a caramel apple on a stick. Considering the age statement of less than five years, the nose is remarkably good, with none of the harsher notes that can sometimes show up in a younger rye. The specialty malt is particularly apparent here, and it works.

The palate begins with toffee and chocolate milk. Moving toward the mid-palate, chopped hazelnuts join a mild clove note, creating a silky mouthfeel. The initial taste is very much in chocolate candy bar territory, with the toffee and cocoa notes working together nicely.

On the finish, the chocolate becomes less sweet, taking the form of semi-sweet chocolate alongside espresso and nutmeg. A final push of butterscotch hard candy brings the tasting to a close.

From start to finish, the specialty malts are on full display, and they work at every point. The roasty chocolate and coffee notes, along with the toffee and butterscotch, remain present throughout, giving the rye a consistent profile from the first sniff through the finish. It is simply good drinking.

At less than five years old, this is a highly enjoyable rye that is very well done and certainly deserving of annual special release status. As a bottled-in-bond release, the 100 proof suits it perfectly.

100 proof.

A / $60

title: Review: Nock Tequila and Mezcal, Complete Lineup
summary:
Although the Nock tequila brand opened in 2010, its current incarnation dates to 2022. That is when CEO Melissa Mathieson along with Master Distiller Daniel Antonio Tuesta Popolizio and Master Mezcalero Miguel Martinez produced the 100% agave, 100% additive free tequilas and mezcals we are trying today. They are starting to get national distribution in…

The post Review: Nock Tequila and Mezcal, Complete Lineup appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Although the Nock tequila brand opened in 2010, its current incarnation dates to 2022. That is when CEO Melissa Mathieson along with Master Distiller Daniel Antonio Tuesta Popolizio and Master Mezcalero Miguel Martinez produced the 100% agave, 100% additive free tequilas and mezcals we are trying today. They are starting to get national distribution in the U.S., so let’s give them a try.

All tequila expressions are 80 proof. NOM 1502.
Both mezcal expressions are 84 proof. NOM 070.

Nock Tequila Blanco Review

The nose of this unaged tequila opens with sweet aromas of fresh cut grass, lemon drop candy, white pepper, roasted agave, and a touch of saline. The palate also opens with sweetness, but here it is a bit heavy handed. Candied lemon peel, white pepper, agave, and some unpleasant earthiness. Also, the notes don’t come together as well as they might. This will be a fine blanco for cocktails that would benefit from its sweetness and lemony character. B / $38

Nock Tequila Reposado Review

After the bold aroma of the blanco, I was surprised to find the reposado so reserved. Very light aromas of agave, caramel, and lemon can be found in the glass. The palate is similarly very light, but after I took a few sips, the tequila’s flavors began to assert themselves, presenting lemon citrus, vanilla, a touch of green pepper, and a chemical note. It seems the tequila’s time in oak tempered the flavors of the blanco, but it only lightly asserted the notes of the wood. As a result, it would not easily stand out in a cocktail, but it doesn’t hold together well enough to drink neat. C / $48

Nock Tequila Añejo Review

Aged 18 months. The wood was pretty tame in the reposado, but it’s playing its hand much more assertively here. Aromas of oak and vanilla pour out of the glass first, followed by some grass, roasted agave, and a slightly astringent medical note. This unpleasant medical note appears right away on the palate, followed by oak and vanilla that help to make up for it. Midpalate also brings some roasted agave notes as well. This is a standard 80 proof tequila, but it tastes hot. It could hold up in a cocktail calling for an añejo tequila. C- / $73

Nock Tequila Cristalino Review

After trying the añejo, the nose on the cristalino is a surprise. The unpleasant note is completely gone, and in its place come subtle aromas of roasted agave, lemon, and grass. Without knowing otherwise, I probably would have guessed this was a blanco. The palate, however, brings the wood, and it is quite nice. Vanilla and oak hit first with lemon following. A bit of brine appears late in the game along with a touch of dark chocolate in the finish. This is my favorite of the Nock tequilas. It would serve nicely on its own or in a cocktail. B+ / $73

Nock Mezcal Joven Review

100% Espadin. Classic Espadin character on both the nose and palate, including bold notes of fresh cut grass, lemon citrus, smoky roasted agave, black pepper, brine, and a light hospital touch. This is a surprisingly assertive yet well integrated mezcal. It’s fairly smoky, but the smoke doesn’t hit all at once. Instead, it wafts among the other notes, weaving through the grass, agave, and citrus. The finish brings fresh cracked pepper and a hospital note, while the brine is light and sits in the background throughout. This is a solid sipping mezcal, but its bold flavors would make it stand out in a cocktail. Lovely. A- / $48

Nock Mezcal Añejo Review

Aged 1 year in ex-bourbon barrels, and the nose is very different. Unaged, it was quite assertive, but now it is muted offering light vanilla, some oak, a bit of agave, and a wisp of smoke. The palate, happily, shows more character. The mezcal notes I enjoyed in the joven are apparent and balance well with the oak. Grass, lemon, roasted agave, black pepper, brine, hospital, and smoke are all there, but now they are rounded out with light caramel and vanilla as well as a touch of oaky tannins on the finish. A- / $76

title: Review: The Paring 2024 Pinot Noir and 2021 Red Blend
summary:
So The Paring is a funny name for a wine brand. Like you, probably, I assumed it was “The Pairing,” like, wine that is to be enjoyed with a meal, a succulent meal. But no, The Paring refers to, well, I’m not entirely sure, as the company behind the Santa Barbara County-based portfolio of wines…

The post Review: The Paring 2024 Pinot Noir and 2021 Red Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
So The Paring is a funny name for a wine brand. Like you, probably, I assumed it was “The Pairing,” like, wine that is to be enjoyed with a meal, a succulent meal. But no, The Paring refers to, well, I’m not entirely sure, as the company behind the Santa Barbara County-based portfolio of wines never really explains it.

The company offers a range of bottlings. Today we check out its pinot noir and red blend, both quite affordable.

2024 The Paring Pinot Noir Santa Barbara County – Santa Barbara fruit aged in 65% French oak (35% new and 65% neutral) for 11 months. Designed to be a bold wine, this is initially a bit overwhelming, this pinot eventually settles into a surprisingly fruity groove, melding blackberry and raspberry into a juicy whole. A dusting of tea leaf and late-game cola evoke more traditional California pinot notes, becoming increasingly emphatic and clove-dusted as they develop in glass over time. Give it a good hour and you’ll find your toes dipping into notes of chocolate and nutmeg. A- / $25

2021 The Paring Red California – A Bordeaux style blend made from 60% Cabernet Sauvignon, 15% Cabernet Franc, 15% Merlot, and 10% Petit Verdot. Aged in French oak, 55% new and 45% neutral, for 22 months. Quite juicy with a nose of currants and some raisin, this dense wine feels more New World than Old, with overtones of milk chocolate and coffee adding even more of a dessert-like vibe, at least until the rather tannic conclusion arrives. Significant tannins perk their head up on the finish, however, wiping away much of the sweetness and leaving the palate coated in notes of black tea and dried herbs. An oddity, for sure. B / $25

title: Review: Larrikin Single Barrel Rye 9 Years Old
summary:
Larrikin Bourbon Co. was founded by Greg Neeley, a former officer in both the Royal Australian Navy and the United States Navy. The name comes from an Australian term with a long history. During the 1860s and 1870s, “larrikin” referred to a young hooligan or troublemaker, often associated with working-class men, drinking, fighting, and a…

The post Review: Larrikin Single Barrel Rye 9 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Larrikin Bourbon Co. was founded by Greg Neeley, a former officer in both the Royal Australian Navy and the United States Navy. The name comes from an Australian term with a long history. During the 1860s and 1870s, “larrikin” referred to a young hooligan or troublemaker, often associated with working-class men, drinking, fighting, and a general disregard for authority. By the early 20th century, the word had taken on a more affectionate meaning. The archetypal larrikin became the irreverent Australian who disliked pretension, authority, and excessive formality. Mischievous and independent, the larrikin was not necessarily malicious.

During World War I, the image became closely associated with the Australian soldier, particularly members of the Australian Imperial Force (AIF). Australian troops were portrayed as rough, irreverent, resourceful, and willing to challenge authority. The larrikin became a more positive figure, representing someone willing to take an unconventional route to get the job done.

Based in Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, Larrikin Bourbon Co. has built a following through releases sourced from an assortment of distilleries. In the summer of 2026, the company released Larrikin Single Barrel Rye Whiskey 9 Years Old, distilled and aged in Bardstown, Kentucky. The whiskey was made from a mashbill of 64% rye, 30% corn, and 6% malted barley.

The origin of the rye remains officially undisclosed, but there is a connection to Nelson’s Green Brier. In 2016, Nashville’s Nelson’s Green Brier contracted Bardstown Bourbon Company to distill this exact mashbill. The resulting barrel heads were stamped “Belle Meade Rye” and “DSP KY-20037.”

The Nelson family resurrected the Belle Meade Bourbon brand in 2012 at Nelson’s Green Brier, using a mashbill of 64% corn, 30% rye, and 6% malted barley. In that recipe, the corn and rye percentages are reversed from those found in Larrikin’s rye whiskey.

Despite the “Belle Meade Rye” markings on the barrel heads, Belle Meade Rye was never released under that name. Nelson Brothers Straight Rye, however, uses the same mashbill. The house brand from Nelson’s Green Brier first appeared in 2023 and was bottled at 92.5 proof.

At 9 years old and 122.5 proof, Larrikin’s Single Barrel Rye brings additional age and considerably more proof to the same foundation represented by Nelson Brothers Straight Rye.

So, what does Larrikin’s nine-year-old rye bring to the glass?

Larrikin Single Barrel Rye 9 Years Old (2026) Review

The nose opens with a clear impression of orange Jell-O, followed by fresh sourdough bread that remains present in the glass. Given more time, fresh mint appears, followed later by under-ripe plums. It is one of the more interesting rye whiskey noses I’ve experienced in quite some time, even if its overall potency is somewhat limited.

That lack of potency on the nose is not an issue on the palate. Tangerine arrives immediately, followed by cinnamon as the citrus subsides. The mid-palate then moves toward Sour Patch Kids candy and glazed yeast donuts, with the latter tying back nicely to the sourdough note found on the nose. The palate is considerably more expressive than the nose suggests, offering far more intensity and range than the initial aroma might lead you to expect.

The finish brings ginger and an ever so slight touch of maple syrup before moving into the hot bite of sliced radish. That radish note quickly gives way to the sweet citrus profile of Sunny Delight orange drink.

For those who enjoy bright, zesty rye whiskeys, the palate and finish deliver exactly what you are looking for, all without the amount of oak influence one might expect from the age statement. In the mouth, the whiskey has medium viscosity and plenty of flavor. I simply wish the nose offered a little more expression to match what follows.

122.5 proof.

A- / $120

title: Review: NV Tabor Hill Blanc de Noir and Rosso di Lago
summary:
Few people associate Michigan with wine country, but the Tabor Hill Winery in the Lake Michigan Shore AVA has a fifty-year history of winemaking. They produce a range of offerings, including multiple varieties of reds, whites, sparkling, and fruit wines. Today we are trying two special new releases, including one white and one red, both…

content:
Few people associate Michigan with wine country, but the Tabor Hill Winery in the Lake Michigan Shore AVA has a fifty-year history of winemaking. They produce a range of offerings, including multiple varieties of reds, whites, sparkling, and fruit wines. Today we are trying two special new releases, including one white and one red, both made entirely with estate grown fruit. Let’s give them a try.

NV Tabor Hill Blanc de Noir – This is an uncommon style of wine made with pinot noir grapes but with minimal skin contact after pressing, which produces a white wine. The nose is reserved at first, but with time it becomes very nice, offering fleshy peach, orange peel, frothy cream, a floral note, and a bit of perfume. The palate follows suit with an Orange Julius note coming first followed by peach, lemon peel, and perfume. The wine has low to medium acidity and a fairly long finish. It will pair well with light fare including baked chicken and vegetables, but it is delightful on its own. As we’re moving into the holiday season, I think it would go perfectly with Thanksgiving turkey and stuffing. B+ / $45

NV Tabor Hill Rosso di Lago – Made in the style of an Italian Super Tuscan, this wine includes sangiovese, merlot, syrah, and cabernet sauvignon, and it is aged for a year in French and Hungarian oak. I’m surprised the wine doesn’t list the year grapes were harvested since the tannic varieties that make up the wine typically need time in the bottle to reach their peak. Poured in a glass, the wine is uninspiring, smelling like boozy grape juice with a pronounced herbal note of sage. Happily, the palate is more enjoyable with the herbal note still playing a big part, but it is balanced by blueberry, red currant, cranberry, and blackberry notes. The wine is quite dry, but fruity and tangy. Medium to high acidity and drying tannins provide a nice structure. I wasn’t optimistic when I first smelled this wine, but with a bit of time it shows nice character and complexity. I wouldn’t mistake it for a Super Tuscan, but I’d be happy to drink it alongside a steak or even a cheeseburger. B / $47

content:
There is a certain expectation that whiskey should remain whiskey, that a bottle ought to concern itself with what is inside it and leave politics at the door. I understand the appeal. For many people, bourbon is an escape from the daily arguments of American life, and the idea of keeping politics out of the glass has an obvious draw.

There is just one problem with that idea: American beverage alcohol has never really been separate from politics.

From whiskey and bourbon to beer, wine, vodka and brandy, alcohol has repeatedly found itself caught up in the political arguments of the day. The issues have changed, but the relationship has remained. Taxes, trade, immigration, religion, race, gender, public health, consumer protection, urbanization, rural life and the role of government have all found their way into debates over what Americans drink, who may sell it, how it should be made and what should appear on the bottle.

The history of temperance alone makes that difficult to dispute. The movement that eventually helped bring about national Prohibition was not a brief campaign against drinking. It developed over roughly a century, beginning with early nineteenth-century temperance societies and gradually moving from calls for moderation toward total abstinence and, eventually, government prohibition. The American Temperance Society was founded in 1826, and by the late 1830s the movement was advocating abstinence from all alcoholic beverages. By the middle of the nineteenth century, prohibition had become a legislative issue, with at least 14 states adopting prohibition laws in some form by 1855.

Temperance was also tied to the major political and social divisions of its time. Protestant religious reform was central to much of the movement, while women became some of its most active organizers at a time when most women could not vote. Immigration and anti-Catholic sentiment became part of the debate as reformers criticized drinking customs associated with Irish, German, Italian and other immigrant communities. Industrialization and urbanization brought another set of arguments, with reformers attacking the saloon as a source of disorder, while employers sometimes supported temperance in the name of workplace productivity and safety. African American reformers and organizations also participated in temperance campaigns, although their reasons and political goals were not always the same as those of white prohibitionists.

Race was particularly ugly territory. In the post-Civil War South, anti-alcohol rhetoric was frequently intertwined with white-supremacist politics and the mythology surrounding Black men, sexual violence and white women. Temperance advocates and other political figures sometimes portrayed alcohol as a force that supposedly made Black men dangerous, while whiskey and the saloon became part of a larger argument about race, voting rights and social control. Frances Willard, one of the most prominent temperance leaders of the era, made racist claims about Black voters and drinking in an 1890 interview, linking whiskey, Black political participation and threats to white women.

The rhetoric also appeared in alcohol advertising and political imagery. The Library of Congress holds nineteenth-century whiskey advertisements and labels featuring caricatures of African Americans, among other subjects. In the South, temperance literature and liquor advertising could intersect with the poisonous racial mythology that portrayed Black men as sexually dangerous when drinking. Historical research has documented liquor advertisements that were attacked by white temperance advocates precisely because they depicted white women in ways those advocates claimed would incite Black men.

So political imagery on a whiskey bottle is hardly a new development. Neither is the use of alcohol as a vehicle for arguments about American identity.

The politics also reached the federal government and the regulation of what went into the bottle. The Bottled-in-Bond legislation of 1897 is a useful example. The law grew out of disputes involving adulteration, consumer confidence, taxation, American whiskey’s competition with imported spirits and the interests of distillers, rectifiers and wholesalers. Its passage followed extensive debate in Congress and lobbying from competing segments of the liquor trade. The resulting system placed bonded whiskey under federal supervision and provided consumers with a way to identify spirits made under prescribed conditions.

The Pure Food and Drugs Act of 1906 brought another major political fight over what Americans were entitled to know about the products they purchased. The law prohibited interstate commerce in adulterated and misbranded foods, drugs, drinks and liquors. It was the result of more than two decades of legislative attempts, public agitation, scientific investigation and political pressure. The House of Representatives passed the measure 240 to 17, and President Theodore Roosevelt signed it on June 30, 1906.

Alcohol was therefore not merely sitting on the sidelines while American consumer law developed. Whiskey producers, liquor dealers, temperance advocates, politicians, scientists and reformers were all arguing over what should be sold, how it should be labeled and how much authority the government should have over the marketplace.

And then there was Prohibition itself.

The Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act represented the culmination of decades of political organizing, religious activism, lobbying and electoral campaigning. Prohibition was not simply a referendum on whether Americans should drink. It was bound up with arguments over morality, immigration, race, gender, religion, federal power and the proper role of government. During the 1920s, the Ku Klux Klan also became an important force in Prohibition enforcement, using political pressure and, at times, vigilante methods. Historians have documented the relationship between the Klan and the broader dry movement, even as the Anti-Saloon League maintained its own political organization and denied some of the connections attributed to it.

Political cartoons, newspaper illustrations, advertisements, bottle labels and promotional material provided another outlet for those arguments. Alcohol appeared again and again in the visual record of American political life, whether the subject was temperance, immigration, race, urban vice, public morality, taxation or consumer protection. The bottle was often more than a container. It could also serve as a small billboard for a set of ideas.

That history matters when considering two contemporary bottles that make no attempt to hide their politics.

Blue State Spirits describes itself as a proudly progressive spirits company built around progress, conversation and political satire. Its stated mission centers on community, diversity, accountability and forward thinking, with the bottles intended to say something about the world around them as well as the liquid inside.

That puts Tax the Rich Bourbon and Felon Vodka squarely within a very old American tradition. Tax the Rich features the words “No Kings” alongside its political branding. Felon Vodka goes even further, placing an image of Donald Trump in an orange prison jumpsuit behind bars, a reference to his status as a convicted felon.

There is no real mystery about what either bottle is trying to say. The politics are right there on the label.

Blue State Spirits provided Drinkhacker with a bottle of Tax the Rich Bourbon and Felon Vodka for an unbiased review. Both bottles are likely to attract attention because of their political branding. The more interesting question, at least for the purposes of a spirits review, is what happens after the bottle is opened.

That is where the politics stop and the liquid gets its turn.

Tax the Rich Bourbon Review

Tax the Rich is a six-barrel blend distilled by Bardstown Bourbon Company from a mash bill of 68% corn, 20% wheat, and 12% malted barley. All six barrels come from Lot #20H11, filled on August 11, 2020, and dumped for blending on June 4, 2026, giving the bourbon a total maturation of 5 years, 9 months, and 24 days. The barrels were coopered by Independent Stave Co. with a #4 char and aged in palletized storage.

The nose opens with butterscotch hard candy discs, followed by juicy, ripe peaches with the peach fuzz intact. Waxy honeycomb and almond butter add to the sweet side of the profile. Spice is not a major factor here, with the nose favoring moderate sweetness instead. It is not an especially intricate nose, but it should appeal to a broad range of bourbon drinkers.

On the palate, vanilla pudding skin and toffee arrive first, followed by salted butter and almonds through the mid-palate. The mouthfeel falls just short of medium viscosity, with very little ethanol burn.

The finish brings a bit more going on, starting with light cinnamon before white pepper increases the heat. White pepper remains the primary note through the finish, mingling with honey graham crackers and light oak.

There is nothing off-putting about this bourbon. It is not an especially intricate pour, but it is enjoyable and serves its purpose. Those inclined to purchase Tax the Rich are probably not doing so in anticipation of a top-shelf bourbon. The appeal is largely tied to the story and the conversation that surrounds the bottle, and that comes with a bourbon that is more than capable of holding up its end of the bargain.

At $40, the price also works. Many political-theme bourbons currently on the market come with considerably higher price tags and less time in the barrel. If the goal is to spend $40 on a bottle that provides plenty to talk about while delivering a perfectly serviceable bourbon, there is little reason for regret. 92 proof. B / $40

Felon Vodka Review

Felon is distilled from a 100% corn mashbill by Golden Triangle in Craig, Missouri, with fermentation reaching 17 to 18% abv. A three-column system is used to distill the spirit, which reaches 190 proof. The vodka is Kosher certified at distillation, although Blue State Spirits did not maintain that certification through proofing and bottling.

The nose is light and clean, offering vanilla bean, toasted marshmallow, and faint grain. A slight floral note develops beneath the sweetness, accompanied by a small thread of ethanol.

The palate is soft and slightly sweet on entry, with a relatively neutral profile that gives way to faint grain and black pepper. For vodka, the mouthfeel is surprisingly full, with a slightly oily quality and medium body. A modest alcohol warmth develops through the mid-palate without becoming too hot.

The finish is short to medium in length, with mild warmth, dry grain, and a touch of sweetness reminiscent of candy corn. The alcohol gradually fades without leaving a harsh or bitter note.

Overall, Felon is a clean, approachable corn vodka that favors softness and sweetness rather than complexity. Vanilla, marshmallow, and grain give it more personality than the “neutral” designation might suggest. It is not an especially complex or memorable vodka, but its clean distillation, pleasant mouthfeel, and relatively soft finish make it considerably more enjoyable neat than its price point might suggest. 94 proof. B / $25
